title: Political Economy of Solid Minerals Governance in Nasarawa State, Nigeria: A Rentier State Analysis (1999-2020)
existing_coverage: The wiki has a resource-rent/resource-curse research cluster — research/sachs-warner-resource-curse.md, research/martinez-colombia-resource-rents.md (local-level resource curse in Colombia), research/acemoglu-johnson-robinson-botswana.md (a resource-curse counterexample), concepts/resource-rents.md, and objections/rent-revenue-breeds-corruption.md — but nothing on Nigeria, subnational mineral governance, or the specific mechanism of federal oil-revenue dependence crowding out subnational mineral-rent capture.
reasoning: This is a peer-reviewed mixed-methods study (400-respondent survey, interviews, documentary analysis) applying Rentier State Theory to a concrete subnational case: Nigeria's federal government retains mineral ownership/licensing while Nasarawa State, dependent on oil-revenue transfers, has no incentive to build mineral-governance capacity of its own. It adds a genuinely new case to the resource-curse cluster — subnational/federal rent-dependency dynamics distinct from the Colombia and Botswana cases already on the wiki — and is directly relevant to the Georgist question of who captures resource rent and how governance incentives shift when rent is redistributed rather than locally collected.
source_notes: Innocent Benjamin Namo, Lhebade Agwadu, Attah Henry Attah, Grace Chundung Namo (Nigerian universities), International Journal of Latest Technology in Engineering, Management & Applied Science, vol. 15(6), pp. 2344-2354, published 18 July 2026. Mixed-methods study (400-respondent survey across 13 mining-affected LGAs, 376 usable responses, plus interviews and documentary analysis) finding Nasarawa State functions only as a 'corporate actor and revenue collector,' not a regulator, of its abundant solid-mineral resources, because federal control over mineral ownership/licensing plus dependence on federation-account oil transfers gives the state little incentive to build mineral-revenue capacity — explaining the paradox of mineral abundance alongside underdevelopment. Recommends reforms strengthening state capacity, transparency, and derivation incentives.

title: Extractive fiscal governance and subnational SDG progress: a systemic analysis of mining canon redistribution in Peru, 2012-2024
existing_coverage: No dedicated places/peru.md page exists, and no wiki coverage of Peru's mining canon (royalty-transfer) system. The nearest neighbors are the general resource-rent/resource-curse cluster (research/sachs-warner-resource-curse.md, research/martinez-colombia-resource-rents.md, concepts/resource-rents.md) and research/lincoln-institute-latam-property-tax-book.md for Latin American fiscal context, but none address mining canon specifically.
reasoning: This is a rigorous 13-year panel study (23 regions, 299 observations, fixed-effects models) with a clear, quotable finding directly on point for Georgist resource-rent-capture debates: Peru's mining canon transfers show no statistically significant poverty reduction overall, canon effects concentrate 8x more strongly where mining is already intensive (rewarding extraction locations rather than need), and formal mining employment paradoxically correlates with higher local poverty (enclave dynamics). This nuances the wiki's resource-rent-capture-works benefit claim by showing that rent redistribution design (territorial equity, price-cycle stabilization, institutional capacity) matters as much as the fact of capture — a valuable complication alongside the Colombia and Botswana cases already cited.
source_notes: Emilio J. Medrano-Sanchez (Universidad Tecnológica del Perú) and Alfredo Mamani-Salinas (University of Calgary), Frontiers in Political Science, vol. 8, published 2 July 2026. Fixed-effects panel analysis of Peru's mining canon (royalty redistribution to regions), 23 regions x 2012-2024 (299 observations). Main result: canon transfers show a negative but statistically insignificant association with regional poverty overall (β=-0.074, p=0.530); the effect is ~8x larger in high- vs low-mining-intensity regions (concentrating benefit where extraction already occurs); only the 2017-2019 moderate-price period shows a significant effect; formal mining employment correlates positively with poverty (β=+0.930, p=0.070), consistent with extractive-enclave dynamics. Confirms a 'subnational resource curse' and recommends redistribution reform, stabilization funds, and capacity investment.

title: Review of Patrick M. Condon's Broken City: Land Speculation, Inequality, and Urban Crisis
existing_coverage: Condon's book itself has no dedicated books/ page on the wiki, but organizations/henry-george-foundation-canada.md already mentions a different review of the same book (Francis K. Peddle's Nov 2024 review). No other Broken City coverage found.
reasoning: The underlying book is explicitly Georgist — Condon 'draws on Henry George's theories' and argues 'the public, rather than private owners, should capture the increase in land prices stimulated by economic growth' — yet the wiki has no books/ page for it at all, only a passing mention of a different review. A peer-reviewed IJURR review by a major urban-planning scholar (Susan Fainstein) is a strong occasion to create the book page itself (books/condon-broken-city.md), using the review both to characterize the book's argument and to carry a balanced 'Reception' section (Fainstein's qualified praise plus her critique that the book underweights supply-side factors and Lincoln Institute value-capture literature).
source_notes: Reviewer Susan S. Fainstein (Harvard), International Journal of Urban and Regional Research, published 31 Oct 2025, reviewing Patrick M. Condon's Broken City: Land Speculation, Inequality, and Urban Crisis (2024). Fainstein calls it 'a worthwhile contribution to the housing literature' and 'highly suitable for class assignment,' praising Condon's clear central thesis that land-value speculation, not regulatory restriction, drives housing crises, and that the public should capture land-price increases generated by growth rather than private owners keeping them (explicitly Georgist framing). Her critique: the book 'perhaps minimizes the supply problem,' overlooks Harvey/Lefebvre/Smith urban-geography scholarship, and underengages the Lincoln Institute's land-trust and value-capture literature.

title: China's Land Finance as Active Mode of Land Development and Infrastructure Delivery: Reality, History and Prospects
existing_coverage: Two related China land-policy pages already exist: research/xu-huang-li-china-hcrs-george.md (2026, on whether Henry George inspired China's Household Contract Responsibility System — a different Xu, and a different argument about deep-structure parallels) and research/gaffney-real-assets-model-china.md (Gaffney's 2015 boom-bust model applied to China/2008 crash). Neither addresses land finance mechanics (how local governments finance infrastructure via land leasing) directly.
reasoning: This paper explicitly engages Georgist value-capture theory by name — the author argues China's land-finance model is a rare real-world case of the 'active' Georgist approach (public authorities organizing/financing development and capturing land-value increases directly) versus the 'passive' approach dominant in most developing countries, and proposes the Chinese government extend this to capture value from property reselling/redevelopment and fund social spending. This is a distinct contribution from the existing xu-huang-li HCRS paper (which is about rural land tenure, not municipal land finance) and from Gaffney's macro boom-bust model, filling a real gap on how China's land-value-capture actually functions institutionally.
source_notes: Nannan Xu, International Journal of Urban and Regional Research, vol. 50, pp. 191-220, published online 5 Oct 2025 (print Jan 2026). Abstract (Crossref, full text): argues that while most developing countries follow a 'passive' land-development approach (private developers finance/organize development and capture value increases, due to weak state capacity and developer-official coalitions), China became an outlier by transforming into an 'active' Georgist-style approach where the central government's policymaking dismantled the passive equilibrium and let public authorities organize/finance development and capture land-value increases directly. The author credits this to Chinese central-government policy design and recommends China continue and extend Georgist value capture — including to property reselling/redevelopment gains — and use more land revenue for social spending (senior care, child benefits).

title: Paving the way towards predistribution: a study on the introduction of a land value tax
existing_coverage: No places/spain.md page exists. research/blanco-spain-two-lands.md covers a century-long Spanish wealth-composition study (1900-2014, land's share of national wealth) but not any LVT policy proposal or simulation. No Basque Country or Bizkaia coverage found anywhere on the wiki.
reasoning: This is a rigorous, quantified LVT implementation simulation for a real fiscally-autonomous jurisdiction (Bizkaia, Spain's Basque province) — a hedonic spatial model estimating a 1.05% land-value tax rate sufficient to replace existing real-estate and lower-90th-percentile income taxes, framed explicitly around predistribution vs. redistribution. This is genuinely new: no Spain/Basque LVT coverage exists on the wiki at all, and it belongs in the same genre as the wiki's other jurisdiction-specific LVT simulation studies (e.g., the Cincinnati/South Bend/Princeton parcel-simulation series already on the wiki).
source_notes: Jesús Olea, David Hoyos, Javier García Enríquez (University of the Basque Country), The Annals of Regional Science, published online 17 Feb 2025 (print March 2025). Abstract (Crossref, full text): simulates an LVT for Bizkaia (a Spanish province with fiscal autonomy) that would displace existing real-estate taxes and partially displace income tax, as a first step toward ecological tax reform. Uses a spatially-correlated hedonic price model to estimate the tax base; following Lyons (2012), sets the collection target as the amount from shifting all real-estate taxes plus income-tax returns of the lowest-taxable-base ~75% of the population, then computes average tax per square metre. Finds a proportional rate of 1.05% on land value would suffice for the proposed tax shift, and concludes that focusing fiscal policy on predistribution (rather than redistribution) may support a more sustainable and fair economy.
